329 AM EST Tue Nov 17 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Added a key message to address the potential low pressure system
that could possibly impact the region Sunday into Monday. 

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Dry and warm conditions expected through the end of the 
  week.

- 2) Increasing confidence in a low pressure system developing 
  in the southeast this weekend, potentially impacting our 
  region Sunday into Monday. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and warm conditions expected through the end of
the week.

High pressure will build over the central Plains in the upper 
levels, while transitioning to a surface high pressure over the 
mid-Atlantic. This ridge will result in very dry conditions and 
gradually increasing temperatures through the rest of the week. 
Plenty of sunshine each day with highs approaching the middle to
upper 60s to near 70 by Friday across the region. Lows at night
will remain in the 30s to 40s through the week. One caveat to 
the prolonged dry conditions and warming temperatures could have
implications on fire weather (see Fire Weather section below). 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Increasing confidence in a low pressure system 
developing in the southeast this weekend, potentially impacting 
our region Sunday into Monday. 

A piece of shortwave energy, loosely connected to the trough 
that moved offshore last week, will be spinning over the 
southeast CONUS/Gulf Coast region. This likely gets pushed off 
to our south and east with little impact towards the end of the 
week. Depending on what model guidance you look at though, this
could even play a role later in the week, so thought I'd mention
it here just to have it in the broader picture. What is more 
interesting to watch for our area is what comes in behind it. 
The subtropical jet shows signs of becoming active during this 
late week/weekend timeframe. Virtually all guidance now develops
a closed upper low somewhere along the Gulf Coast/Southeast 
Atlantic coast by late Saturday/early Sunday. There will also be
a very potent upper trough and attendant surface low across the
central CONUS, which is currently over the Gulf of Alaska. The 
evolution of this low pressure system will play a pivotal role 
in where the low over the southeast coast ends up going. 

This is where details get very murky. Without getting into the
specifics of each model, there is a solution that shows about 
any low track you could think of. The ultimate track of the low
is going to depend on exactly when and where it forms, which is
just information we do not have at this point. Ensemble guidance
is all over the place, with tracks ranging from up the
Appalachian mountains to well offshore. For now, this is just 
something to monitor closely in the coming days. 

It is important to note that a majority of the relevant pieces 
of energy that need to develop for this system to form are 
still not being well-sampled into model data, as they remain 
offshore or haven't developed at all. However, that will change
over the next 24 to 36 hours, so stay tuned to the latest
forecast as this potential system unfolds. 

&&

.AVIATION /07Z TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Mainly dry for all TAF sites through the upcoming week. VFR 
conditions are anticipated through the end of the week as high 
pressure remains in control. Skies should remain mostly clear, 
with winds staying below 10 knots generally. Winds generally 
flow WSW before shifting northwesterly Friday.

&&

.MARINE...
Winds become light and variable to calm at times through much 
of this week. Winds are expected to shift southerly by Thursday
night before shifting back to the north on Friday, generally 
staying below 10 knots.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
High pressure gradually builds overhead through the middle of the
week, then temperatures will begin to warm mid to late week. 
During this timeframe, while winds will diminish, RH values will 
go down substantially. The dry air really builds in starting 
today into tonight, and looks to continue for several days 
thereafter. Overnight recoveries, especially on the ridges, will 
likely be very poor as well starting tonight. Expect afternoon RH
values to drop well into the teens and 20s each day west of the 
Blue Ridge, and the 20s to 30s east of the Blue Ridge. This will 
also be paired with seasonably warm temperatures, so this will 
really act to dry out already very dry fuels.

Not helping matters is that there is no precipitation expected 
east of the Appalachians through at least the end of the week. 
Given the setup, will really be watching for any potential dry 
frontal passages in the long range as the next days to really 
watch out for. Watching late weekend into early next week for the
next weather system, but unsure what it will bring at this point.
While precipitation is possible, it could also bring a dry frontal
passage instead. Continue to monitor the latest forecast as this
timeframe approaches.
